3. Facts disclosed in the petition traced his career since he joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon in 1952 till he became the Director of the Institute in 1972. After getting several promotions since he joined service he was confirmed as Professor of Medicine on April 24, 1963, Besides performing his duties he carried on research in Medical Science and published a number of articles and also books. In 1965 the appellant was appointed the Joint Director of the Institute and in March, 1967 was appointed to act as Professor of Medicine in addition to his duties as Joint Director.

Referring to his ability as a reputed doctor and his academic performance which are not disputed by the respondents, the learned Counsel submitted that in such background there cannot be even any possibility for thinking that the appellant had been retired on the ground of inefficiency, negligence or misconduct in the performance of his duties. After obtaining the degree of M.B. from the University of Calcutta the appellant joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon on April 10, 1952. He obtained T.D.D. degree from the University of Wales and M.R.C.P. degree from Edinburgh. He was appointed Professor of Medicine 1962 and was confirmed in this post in 1963. He got to his credit the publication of a number of articles and books in the field of medical sentence and in recognition thereof he was made F.R.C.P. (London). While the appellant was serving as Professor of Medicine in the Chittagong Medical College he was appointed to act as the Joint Director of the Institute. On March 31, 1967 he was appointed as Professor of Medicine in the Institute in addition to his duties as Joint Director. When in March, 1970 Sir James Cameron, the Director, who was also a Professor of Medicine of the Institute, left for the United Kingdom, the appellant was put in charge of the Office of the Director of the Institute in addition to his duties as the Joint Director and Professor of Medicine.

 33. In distinguishing the decision pronounced by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Jibendra Kishore Achhara Chowdhury vs. The Province of East Pakistan. (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 21= PLD 1957 SC 9, Munir, C.J. observed that no analogy could be drawn between the impugned provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulations Act and the provisions of the E. Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, whose constitutionality was challenged in the aforesaid case. The provisions of this Act which were impugned were held to be not unconstitutional as they had intended to eliminate all rent-receiving interests and to create a uniform class of tenants under the Government and that section 3 of the Act gave the power or discretion to acquire simultaneously or from time to time, the interests which were to be terminated. In rejecting the contentions that the Act in question Jibendra Kishor Achharya Chowdhury's case was on the face of it discriminatory, the Supreme Court held that: 

 74. After having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) violated Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, I am of the view that since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules containing them provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a government servant from amongst a group of government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion. It was not the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the government cannot have or claim the power to retire a government servant after the completion of 25 years of service, though the age of superannuation has been fixed at 57, but what is of importance and consequence to the government servant concerned who is proposed to be retired on completion of 25 years of service is that the discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2, East Bengal Service Rule and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973. Where such basis has been provided by the enunciation of such principles, whether, under the Act or Rules made under an Act or even in the note to such Rules regarding the retirement of government servants, the concerned authority before exercising its discretion, has to con-form to the principles so provided therein, Such principles may be elaborately stated, as in rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973, but even if the rules made under an Act or note appended to any rules providing retirement on the completion of 25 years merely mention that the service of such government servant who has completed 25 years is not necessary in the interest of public service or in public interest, some basis for classification or selection is discernible. Where such basis has been provided, if the government servant concerned challenges the action of government in retiring him on completion of 25 years what the Government has to do is to show that his retirement was necessary in public interest or in the interest of public service. On the other hand, the provisions of section 9(2) coupled with the omission of such basis in the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975 leaves scope to the concerned authority to arbitrarily retire a government servant who has completed 25 years of service. Had the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules. 1975 provided principles as embodied in Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants ( Retirement) Rules, 1973 which were made under similar provisions of law as in section 9(2) of the Act, no challenge could perhaps have been made as to the constitutionality of the impugned provisions of this section. The existence of such principles as are found in the Rules of 1973 would have provided a complete answer to any such challenge to their constitutionality, in spite of the expression "without assigning any reason" used in section 9(2) of the Act. In such a case the authority concerned would have remained free, so as not to disclose any reason in the retirement order, but if its action in retiring a government servant was challenged as arbitrary as has been done by the appellant in the present case, the authority could have disclosed before the Court the basis of its action, 

 80. Appellant's case in short is that after obtaining M.B. degree from the Calcutta. University he joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon on April 10, 1952. While in service, the appellant obtained T.O.D. degree from the University of Wales and M.R.C.P. degree from Edinburg and by successive promotions he became the Professor of Medicine in 1962. On the recommendation of the Public Service Commission he was confirmed as Professor of Medicine on May 10, 1963 with effect from April 24, 1963. The appellant stated that in recognition of his academic excellence and scientific contributions in medicine he was awarded F.R.C.P London under a special clause, as he was not an M.R. C.P. of London by examination. While the appellant was serving as Professor of Medicine in the Chittagong Medical College he was appointed to act as the Joint Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Later on the Government by the Notification dated March 31, 1967 appointed him to act as Professor of Medicine of the said Institute in addition to his duties as Joint Director. In March, 1968 Sir James Cameron, who was the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research since establishment of the Institution in 1965, left for the U.K. and appellant was put in charge of the office of the Director and Professor of Medicine by the Notification dated January 5, 1972; and by the Notification dated November 24, 1972 the appellant was appointed as the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research with effect from January 9, 1971. Appellant's further case is that due, to his meritorious service, the Government granted him the ad-hoc rank and status of Joint Secretary in 1974; and in 1975 he was given the ad-hoc rank and status of Additional Secretary During the period of 1974-75 he was the Personal Physician of the then President of Bangladesh. The appellant stated that he completed 25 years of service on April 10, 1977 By Notification No. Per 1/1M-35/78/951 dated November 22, 1978 he was relieved of his duties and designation of Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Legality of the Notification was challenged by filing a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division by its judgment dated December 6, 1979 declared the Notification dated Nov. 22, 1978 to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. In view of the said declaration the appellant was restored to the position held by him, that is, Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute. Appellant's grievance is that having failed to dislodge the appellant by the Notification dated November 22, 1978 the Government issued the impugned Notification dated June 5, 1980 purporting to retire the appellant from service in exercise of the power conferred under sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974. Legality of this Notification has been challenged on the ground of the order being in contravention of the constitutional protections, and also on the ground of malafide alleging that the impugned Notification is in furtherance and fulfilment of the illegal design of not only circumventing the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 but also achieving ulterior purpose.
